To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

insulin infused into MBH in rats increases lipogenic gene expression and suppresses lipolytic gene expression in WAT, and that mice lacking neuronal insulin receptors exhibit unrestrained lipolytic gene activity and decreased lipogenic gene activity in WAT.
insulin infused into MBH of Sprague-Dale rats increases WAT protein expression, inactivate hormone sensitive lipase and suppress lipolysis.
brain insulin controls adipose lipolysis and de novo lipogenesis.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the brain in the control of adipose tissue function.
the effects of brain insulin signaling on the control of lipogenesis and lipolysis in white adipose tissue.
the regulation of adipose tissue lipogenesis and lipolysis by brain insulin.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the brain, and in particular the MBH, controls WAT lipolyses and lipogenesis, and this is mediated by insulin.
brain insulin is required for the maintenance of WAT functionality, and that its deficiency is associated with WAT dysfunction.
brain insulin controls adipose-tissue lipolysis and de novo lipogenesis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
insulin action on WAT lipolipogenesis is regulated by the brain.
brain insulin regulates the metabolic state of adipose tissue and that this regulation is lost in DM2.
brain insulin is an important regulator of WAT lipolysic and lipogenic pathways.
The main takeaway from our work is that
brain insulin controls adipose lipolysis and de novo lipogenesis, thereby regulating systemic glucose homeostasis and preventing the development of DM2.
brain insulin controls WAT lipolipolysis and lipolipogenesis.
insulin action in the brain is a major regulator of WAT metabolism and, thus, a potential therapeutic target to improve WAT function in DM2.
